description:
Named after the Roman goddess of agriculture and the dwarf planet, Ceres links the field with what we see from space. We want to help farmers face a changing climate with smarter crop rotations.
Looking for software developers, UX designers and professionals with agronomic background. This is an opportunity to build something really useful. Contact me!
summary: Ceres helps a farmer or advisor know a field before renting or buying it, based on historical rotations. At its centre is how the field was rotated: you mark the field on your phone and Ceres rebuilds what was grown in each of its last 5 seasons, crossing NASA MODIS vegetation data (250 m, every 16 days) with Argentina's INTA crop map and with what you tell it. It then crosses that history with more NASA data, NASA POWER soil water and rain since 2001 and NASA's MODIS flood maps, to rate the field (Weak, Fair, Good or Top, with how sure it is) and to propose three crop rotations side by side, each with its risk in a dry year and how long it keeps the soil covered. Every number shows its source and date, and the app says "No data" when it does not know. We checked it against independent sources: the history agrees with the INTA crop map in 8 of 8 season parts, and in the seasons Ceres labels dry, official Bragado yields were lower. Built from interviews with Argentine producers, for the Pampas. A professional still decides.
details:
CERES

Project link: https://ceres-field-shift.vercel.app/


A rotation tool for the moment the rotation is decided. Field Shift asks for a tool that helps farmers compare crop rotations that improve soil health and resilience. To decide where such a tool helps most, before writing any code we held long conversations with producers from the Argentine farming region. Their answer shaped Ceres.

The rotation changes on land you do not know. On their own land, producers already know how it behaves, and satellite data adds little to that decision. The moment it matters is when they are about to rent or buy a field. Today, the only way to learn how such a field was rotated is to go there in person, and fields of very different quality are often rented as if they were all the same.

Starting from the existing rotation. Ceres helps answer one concrete question: "what is this field I have never farmed, and how should I rotate it?". It follows the challenge in order. Field Shift asks to compare at least three strategies including the existing rotation, and for a rented field nobody hands over that rotation. So Ceres rebuilds it from space first, and then proposes what comes next.

The problems we heard, and what we built for each.

  • Soil water is the missing piece. It is the information producers value most and find least available. NASA POWER root-zone soil water drives the risk of every rotation. It is one value for the area, not by depth, and the app says so.
  • Technology that overstates is worse than none. Producers want a tool to take to the field and compare with what they see, not one that replaces the visit. Every result says how sure it is, Ceres says "No data" when it does not know, and a field visit guide points to the places worth checking on site.
  • Privacy: platforms that keep their data. Producers distrust free tools that ask them to hand over their data. Ceres has no accounts. The fields stay on the phone, only the field outline is sent to fetch the data, and the code is open.
  • Poor signal in the field. The tool is used on a phone, outdoors, often with weak or no internet. Ceres is phone first, works with taps instead of typing, and opens saved fields without a connection.
  • Ask, do not assume. Every field and every farmer is different. Ceres asks what matters most (a dry year, a wet year, caring for the soil) and shows "I assumed this. Change it if it is wrong."
  • Agronomy decides the rotation. Producers rotate by agronomy: alternating legumes and grasses, residue, rain and soil. The three strategies follow written agronomic rules, with the evidence for each.

What we said no to, and what we still do not know. The producers also asked for satellite monitoring of cattle pasture and help keeping farm records. Both are real needs and both are outside this challenge, so we did not build them. We never asked them about floods, which priorities they would choose, how rotation is agreed in a rental contract, or whether three rotations side by side read as we expect. Those stay as assumptions to validate, and a few conversations are a small sample.

What Ceres does, step by step.

  1. Mark the field (draw it, use your location, open a KML or type coordinates) over a recent NASA GIBS image (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2, 30 m, the newest clear date in the last 45 days).
  2. How it was rotated, the centre of the app: for each of the last 5 seasons, a summer crop, a winter crop or bare soil, read from NASA MODIS MOD13Q1 NDVI (250 m, one image every 16 days, through NASA OPeNDAP and CMR). A crop is a growth cycle: NDVI rising above 0.5 and falling back. The crop name comes from the INTA National Crop Map, and the person confirms or corrects each half of every season.
  3. The field's rating: Weak, Fair, Good or Top, with how sure it is, from four points: dry years (MODIS NDVI in the area's dry years), too much water (NASA MODIS flood maps through GIBS), how it was rotated (do crop families alternate, and does no summer crop repeat more than 2 seasons in a row) and soil cover (MODIS). The rule was written before the demo field was read. The demo field rates Good, low confidence: never seen under water, but bare in 31 of the 59 months seen.
  4. Water of the area: out of every 10 seasons, how many were dry, normal and wet, from NASA POWER rain, evapotranspiration and root-zone soil wetness since 2001, plus the soil water when each season started.
  5. What matters to you: the person picks priorities (a dry year, a wet year, caring for the soil and others). When they leave the order as it was, the screen says why.
  6. Three rotations for the next 3 seasons, side by side: two alternatives and "keep as it was", each with its risk in a dry and in a wet year ("X to Y of every 10 years in the past"), months with the soil covered, changes of crop family and a short reason. Crop fit comes from FAO EcoCrop against the NASA POWER climate. The rotations follow written agronomic rules for the Pampas.
  7. Field visit guide: up to 5 points inside the field to check on site, where MODIS cells stayed clearly less or more green than the rest in at least 3 seasons, and a field report to share or print.

How we checked it. We compared what Ceres reads with sources that do not depend on it, and we say where we changed a rule after seeing the data:

  • Field history across Argentina: 48 lots sampled at random in eight farming regions, 2019/20 to 2024/25. 78 of the 86 season halves the satellite could read agree with the INTA crop map: 91% (95% interval 82% to 96%). Always guessing "summer crop, fallow winter" would get 74%. These are lots of a single crop class, the easy case.
  • Dry years against harvests: in the seasons Ceres labels dry, official yields of the Bragado district were lower than in normal ones (second-crop soybean 45% lower, first-crop soybean 15%, maize 11%, wheat 4%). The labels were fixed before we looked at any yield. The miss is 2020/21: dry by its rain, but soybean and maize yielded at or above normal.
  • Dry and wet labels against the record: of 18 seasons with crop and press reports, none clearly disagrees. Every clear drought (2008/09, 2017/18, 2022/23) is labelled dry and every flood season (2001/02, 2012/13, 2016/17, 2024/25) wet. We changed that rule after seeing two disagreements, and we say so.
  • Soil water against a second NASA source: NASA POWER and NASA SMAP L4 agree on drier or wetter than usual in 9 of 11 seasons.
  • One rule written and committed before we ran it failed its own test, so we did not ship it. The full chain also ran on three lots outside Bragado (Pergamino, Marcos Juárez, Río Cuarto), and we wrote down what fails there.

Why it matters. Ceres turns open NASA data into the history and risk of that one field, in plain words, on a phone, at the one moment our producers said satellite data could change a rotation. A field rotated better from the first season is better soil for everyone who farms it next.

What it does not do. It does not decide, and it predicts neither yield, rain nor prices. Climate and soil water are for an area of about 55 × 57 km (one NASA POWER cell), not for the field. The rotation rules are a draft not yet reviewed by an agronomist. On the demo field the three rotations get the same water risk (medium, about 4 in 10 years); the screen says so and leads with what differs. The field's rating rests on the flood maps alone there, so its confidence is low. Live, NASA OPeNDAP does not serve MODIS images before mid-2022, so the public app fills them from a recording of the same NASA files, only for the demo field.

Tools. TypeScript throughout: Next.js and React for the phone web app (installable, with an English and a Spanish version), NestJS for the api (no database), a plain TypeScript engine that runs on the phone, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap for the map. Open source.
